    Stable-agent savings: For agents in the stable variance class (σ^fp2<σlow2\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{\mathrm{fp}}<\sigma^{2}_{\text{low}}), the typical reduction is n∗∈[15,25]n^{*}\in[15,25] compared to nfixed≈100n_{\mathrm{fixed}}\approx 100.

  4. 4.

    Statistical validity: When k≥10k\geq 10 and σ^fp2\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{\mathrm{fp}} is within ±30%\pm 30\% of σtrue2\sigma^{2}_{\mathrm{true}} (which holds with probability ≥0.95\geq 0.95 by the chi-squared concentration bound), the actual error rates remain within [α,1.5​α][\alpha,1.5\alpha] and [β,1.5​β][\beta,1.5\beta].

Proof.

Property (i). The worst-case variance of a dd-dimensional fingerprint with each component in [0,1][0,1] is bounded by σmax2=d/4\sigma^{2}_{\max}=d/4 (each component has variance at most 1/41/4). By definition, σ^fp2≤σmax2\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{\mathrm{fp}}\leq\sigma^{2}_{\max}, so n∗≤nfixedn^{*}\leq n_{\mathrm{fixed}}.

Property (ii). Follows directly from the linear relationship between n∗n^{*} and σ^fp2\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{\mathrm{fp}} in (39), with the fixed-sample formula corresponding to σ^fp2=σmax2\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{\mathrm{fp}}=\sigma^{2}_{\max}.

Property (iii). For stable agents with σ^fp2<0.05\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{\mathrm{fp}}<0.05 and typical deff∈[3,8]d_{\mathrm{eff}}\in[3,8], substituting into (39) with α=0.05\alpha=0.05, β=0.10\beta=0.10, ΔM,min=0.5\Delta_{\mathrm{M,min}}=0.5:

n∗=⌈(1.645+1.282)2×0.050.25+62⌉=⌈1.71+3⌉=5n^{*}=\left\lceil\frac{(1.645+1.282)^{2}\times 0.05}{0.25}+\frac{6}{2}\right\rceil=\left\lceil 1.71+3\right\rceil=5 (40)

With a safety margin of (1+2/k)(1+\sqrt{2/k}) for finite-sample estimation uncertainty (where kk is the calibration size), the practical recommendation is n∗∈[15,25]n^{*}\in[15,25].

Property (iv). The calibration variance σ^fp2\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{\mathrm{fp}} follows a scaled chi-squared distribution: (k−1)​σ^fp2/σtrue2∼χk−12(k-1)\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{\mathrm{fp}}/\sigma^{2}_{\mathrm{true}}\sim\chi^{2}_{k-1}. For k=10k=10, the 95% confidence interval for σtrue2\sigma^{2}_{\mathrm{true}} is:

[(k−1)​σ^fp2χ0.975,k−12,(k−1)​σ^fp2χ0.025,k−12]=[0.51​σ^fp2, 2.30​σ^fp2]\left[\frac{(k-1)\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{\mathrm{fp}}}{\chi^{2}_{0.975,k-1}},\;\frac{(k-1)\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{\mathrm{fp}}}{\chi^{2}_{0.025,k-1}}\right]=[0.51\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{\mathrm{fp}},\;2.30\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{\mathrm{fp}}] (41)

If the true variance exceeds our estimate by a factor of γ=σtrue2/σ^fp2\gamma=\sigma^{2}_{\mathrm{true}}/\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{\mathrm{fp}}, the actual sample size needed is n∗×γn^{*}\times\gamma. We run n∗n^{*} trials, so the effective significance level becomes at most α×γ1/2≤1.5​α\alpha\times\gamma^{1/2}\leq 1.5\alpha for γ≤2.3\gamma\leq 2.3, which holds with probability 0.975. ∎

7.3 Trace-First Offline Analysis

The most dramatic cost reduction comes from the observation that most testing activities do not require new agent executions. If execution traces are already available—from production logging, previous test campaigns, or staging environments—four of the six test types in AgentAssay can execute at zero additional token cost.

Definition 7.5 (Trace Store).

A trace store is a persistent, versioned collection 𝒯store={(τi,xi,vi,ti)}i=1N\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{store}}=\{(\tau_{i},x_{i},v_{i},t_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} of execution traces, where τi\tau_{i} is the trace, xix_{i} the input, viv_{i} the agent version, and tit_{i} the timestamp. A trace store supports two operations:

  • •

    query(v,S)→{τ:vτ=v,xτ∈S}\mathrm{query}(v,S)\to\{\tau:v_{\tau}=v,\;x_{\tau}\in S\}: retrieve traces for version vv matching scenario set SS.

  • •

    sample⁡(v,n)→{τ1,…,τn}\mathrm{sample}(v,n)\to\{\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{n}\}: draw nn traces uniformly at random from version vv’s traces.

Definition 7.6 (Trace-First Testing).

A test type 𝒯\mathcal{T} is trace-first compatible if its verdict can be computed entirely from a set of pre-recorded execution traces without executing the agent. Formally, 𝒯\mathcal{T} is trace-first compatible if there exists a function V𝒯:(𝒯store)∗→{Pass,Fail,Inconclusive}V_{\mathcal{T}}\colon(\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{store}})^{*}\to\{\textsc{Pass}{},\allowbreak\textsc{Fail}{},\allowbreak\textsc{Inconclusive}{}\} such that:

V𝒯​(query⁡(v,S))=V𝒯live​(Av,S)V_{\mathcal{T}}(\mathrm{query}(v,S))=V_{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{live}}(A_{v},S) (42)

when the stored traces are sampled from the same distribution as live executions.

Theorem 7.3 (Trace-First Soundness).

Given a trace store 𝒯store\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{store}} with traces sampled i.i.d. from the production input distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D}, the following properties hold:

  1. 1.

    Coverage soundness. Coverage computed on stored traces is a lower bound on achievable coverage:

    𝒞⁡(𝒯store)≤𝒞∗​(𝒟)\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{store}})\leq\mathcal{C}^{*}(\mathcal{D}) (43)

    where 𝒞∗​(𝒟)\mathcal{C}^{*}(\mathcal{D}) is the coverage achievable with unlimited testing. Equality holds as |𝒯store|→∞|\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{store}}|\to\infty.

  2. 2.

    Contract violation soundness. If a contract violation is detected in a stored trace τi\tau_{i}, then the violation is a true violation:

    ∃τ∈𝒯store:out(τ)⊧̸ϕ⟹ℙx∼𝒟[out(A(x))⊧̸ϕ]>0\exists\,\tau\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{store}}:\mathrm{out}(\tau)\not\models\phi\implies\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[\mathrm{out}(A(x))\not\models\phi]>0 (44)
  3. 3.

    Metamorphic relation soundness. If a metamorphic relation ℛ\mathcal{R} is violated in stored trace pairs, the violation rate is an unbiased estimator of the true violation rate:

    𝔼⁡[q^store]=qtrue​(ℛ,A,𝒟)\mathbb{E}[\hat{q}_{\mathrm{store}}]=q_{\mathrm{true}}(\mathcal{R},A,\mathcal{D}) (45)
  4. 4.

    Regression incompatibility. Regression detection (Definition 3.7) between versions vv and v′v^{\prime} is not trace-first compatible in general, because it requires traces from version v′v^{\prime} which may not yet exist in the store. However, comparing a candidate against stored baseline traces is valid: only the candidate requires new executions.

Proof.

Part (1). Coverage is a monotonically non-decreasing function of the trace set (Theorem 4.1). The stored traces are a subset of all possible traces, so coverage on the subset is a lower bound. As the store grows, the law of large numbers ensures convergence to the true coverage.

Part (2). A stored trace τ\tau was produced by the actual agent AA on a real input x∼𝒟x\sim\mathcal{D}. If out⁡(τ)⊧̸ϕ\mathrm{out}(\tau)\not\models\phi, this is a concrete witness that the agent can violate the contract. Since traces are not fabricated, this is a true violation. The probability statement follows from the fact that the violating input xx was sampled from 𝒟\mathcal{D}, so the support of 𝒟\mathcal{D} contains a violation-inducing input.

Part (3). Since traces are i.i.d. samples from A⁡(x)A(x) with x∼𝒟x\sim\mathcal{D}, the stored trace pairs (constructed by pairing with their metamorphic transforms) yield violations that are i.i.d. Bernoulli random variables with parameter qtrue=ℙx∼𝒟​[¬ℛ⁡(A⁡(x),A⁡(ϕ⁡(x)))]q_{\mathrm{true}}=\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[\neg\mathcal{R}(A(x),A(\phi(x)))]. The sample mean is an unbiased estimator.

Part (4). Regression detection compares AvA_{v} and Av′A_{v^{\prime}}. If v′v^{\prime} is a new version, no traces from Av′A_{v^{\prime}} exist in the store. However, the baseline traces from AvA_{v} are reusable: only the ncn_{c} candidate traces require new executions, halving the live-run cost. ∎

Table 2 summarizes the compatibility. For a typical CI/CD pipeline where the primary question is “has the agent regressed?”, only the regression detection requires live runs—and those runs benefit from Pillars 1 and 2 (fingerprinting and adaptive budgets). Coverage analysis, contract checking, and metamorphic testing all execute on the trace store at zero marginal cost.

7.4 Multi-Fidelity Proxy Testing

In many deployments, the target agent uses an expensive frontier model (e.g., GPT-4o) but a cheaper proxy model (e.g., GPT-4o-mini) exists that exhibits correlated behavior. Multi-fidelity testing exploits this correlation to reduce cost.

Definition 7.7 (Multi-Fidelity Test Configuration).

A multi-fidelity test is a tuple (Me,Mc,ne,nc,ρ)(M_{e},M_{c},\allowbreak n_{e},n_{c},\rho) where:

  • •

    MeM_{e} is the expensive (target) model with per-trial cost cec_{e},

  • •

    McM_{c} is the cheap (proxy) model with per-trial cost ccc_{c} and cc≪cec_{c}\ll c_{e},

  • •

    nen_{e} and ncn_{c} are the number of trials on each model,

  • •

    ρ∈[−1,1]\rho\in[-1,1] is the Pearson correlation between the behavioral fingerprints of the two models: ρ=Corr⁡(F⁡(τe),F⁡(τc))\rho=\mathrm{Corr}(F(\tau_{e}),F(\tau_{c})) where the correlation is computed component-wise and averaged.

Proposition 7.4 (Multi-Fidelity Cost Reduction).

Let AeA_{e} and AcA_{c} be agents using models MeM_{e} and McM_{c} respectively, with behavioral correlation ρ\rho. The optimal allocation (nc∗,ne∗)(n_{c}^{*},n_{e}^{*}) for detecting a regression of Mahalanobis distance ΔM\Delta_{\mathrm{M}} at level (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) is given by minimizing total cost subject to the power constraint:

minne,nc⁡ne​ce+nc​ccs.t.Power⁡(ne,nc,ρ,ΔM)≥1−β\min_{n_{e},n_{c}}\;n_{e}c_{e}+n_{c}c_{c}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\mathrm{Power}(n_{e},n_{c},\rho,\Delta_{\mathrm{M}})\geq 1-\beta (46)

The combined evidence is:

χcombined2=−[ρ⋅log⁡pc+(1−ρ)⋅log⁡pe]\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{combined}}=-2\!\left[\rho\cdot\log p_{c}+(1-\rho)\cdot\log p_{e}\right] (47)

where pcp_{c} and pep_{e} are the pp-values from the proxy and target tests respectively, and the combined statistic follows χcombined2∼χ42\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{combined}}\sim\chi^{2}_{4} under H0H_{0} by the weighted Fisher combination method. (The implementation uses Stouffer’s ZZ-based combination, which is asymptotically equivalent and more robust to extreme pp-values.)

When ρ≥0.6\rho\geq 0.6 and cc/ce≤0.1c_{c}/c_{e}\leq 0.1, the optimal allocation achieves:

ne∗​ce+nc∗​ccnsingle​ce≤1−ρ2+ρ2​(cc/ce)1≤1−ρ2+0.1​ρ2=1−0.9​ρ2\frac{n_{e}^{*}c_{e}+n_{c}^{*}c_{c}}{n_{\mathrm{single}}c_{e}}\leq\frac{1-\rho^{2}+\rho^{2}(c_{c}/c_{e})}{1}\leq 1-\rho^{2}+0.1\rho^{2}=1-0.9\rho^{2} (48)

For ρ=0.8\rho=0.8: cost ratio ≤0.424\leq 0.424 (2.4×\times savings). For ρ=0.9\rho=0.9: cost ratio ≤0.271\leq 0.271 (3.7×\times savings).

Proof sketch.

The proof adapts the multi-fidelity Monte Carlo framework of Peherstorfer et al. [28] to the hypothesis testing setting. The key observation is that the proxy trials provide information about the target model’s behavior proportional to ρ2\rho^{2} (the coefficient of determination). The optimal allocation minimizes cost while maintaining the total effective sample size neff=ne+ρ2​ncn_{\mathrm{eff}}=n_{e}+\rho^{2}n_{c} at the level required for (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) guarantees. The cost bound (48) follows from the Lagrangian optimization with the constraint neff≥nsinglen_{\mathrm{eff}}\geq n_{\mathrm{single}}. The complete derivation is in Section A.4. ∎

7.5 Warm-Start Sequential Testing

When an agent has been tested previously (e.g., in a prior CI/CD run), the results constitute a prior on the agent’s pass-rate distribution. Bayesian updating allows subsequent SPRT runs to start from an informed prior rather than a non-informative one, reducing the number of trials to reach a decision.

Definition 7.8 (Warm-Start SPRT).

Given a prior Beta distribution p∼Beta​(a0,b0)p\sim\text{Beta}(a_{0},b_{0}) derived from n0n_{0} previous trials with k0k_{0} successes (i.e., a0=k0+1a_{0}=k_{0}+1, b0=n0−k0+1b_{0}=n_{0}-k_{0}+1), the warm-start SPRT initializes the log-likelihood ratio at:

Λ0warm=log⁡B⁡(θ−δ,a0,b0)B⁡(θ,a0,b0)\Lambda_{0}^{\mathrm{warm}}=\log\frac{B(\theta-\delta;a_{0},b_{0})}{B(\theta;a_{0},b_{0})} (49)

where B⁡(p,a,b)=pa−1​(1−p)b−1/Beta⁡(a,b)B(p;a,b)=p^{a-1}(1-p)^{b-1}/\mathrm{Beta}(a,b) is the Beta density. The subsequent updates proceed as in Definition 3.9, with boundaries aa and bb unchanged.

Proposition 7.5 (Warm-Start Efficiency).

The warm-start SPRT (Definition 7.8) satisfies:

  1. 1.

    Error control preserved: ℙ⁡[accept ​H1∣H0]≤α\mathbb{P}[\text{accept }H_{1}\mid H_{0}]\leq\alpha and ℙ⁡[accept ​H0∣H1]≤β\mathbb{P}[\text{accept }H_{0}\mid H_{1}]\leq\beta, provided the prior is well-calibrated (the prior was generated from the same agent version or a version with |pv−pv′|≤δ/2|p_{v}-p_{v^{\prime}}|\leq\delta/2).

  2. 2.

    Sample savings:

    𝔼⁡[Nwarm]≤𝔼⁡[Ncold]−|Λ0warm||𝔼⁡[λ1]|\mathbb{E}[N_{\mathrm{warm}}]\leq\mathbb{E}[N_{\mathrm{cold}}]-\frac{|\Lambda_{0}^{\mathrm{warm}}|}{|\mathbb{E}[\lambda_{1}]|} (50)

    where 𝔼⁡[λ1]\mathbb{E}[\lambda_{1}] is the expected per-trial log-likelihood increment. The savings are proportional to the informativeness of the prior |Λ0warm||\Lambda_{0}^{\mathrm{warm}}|.

  3. 3.

    Graceful degradation: If the prior is mis-calibrated (e.g., derived from a different agent version), the error control degrades by at most α′≤α⋅e|Λ0warm|\alpha^{\prime}\leq\alpha\cdot e^{|\Lambda_{0}^{\mathrm{warm}}|}, which remains small when n0n_{0} is moderate (n0≤20n_{0}\leq 20).

Proof sketch.

Part (1) follows from the Bayesian updating interpretation of the SPRT: incorporating a prior is equivalent to starting the random walk at position Λ0warm\Lambda_{0}^{\mathrm{warm}} instead of 00. If the prior is correct (pprior=ptruep_{\mathrm{prior}}=p_{\mathrm{true}}), the stopping boundaries aa and bb still control the error probabilities by Wald’s identity.

Part (2) uses the optional stopping theorem. The expected number of steps to cross a boundary starting from Λ0\Lambda_{0} instead of 00 is reduced by |Λ0|/|𝔼⁡[λ1]||\Lambda_{0}|/|\mathbb{E}[\lambda_{1}]| (the “head start” divided by the average drift rate). The full derivation uses Wald’s equation with a shifted initial condition.

Part (3) bounds the excess error when the prior is wrong. A mis-calibrated prior shifts the initial position by at most |Λ0warm||\Lambda_{0}^{\mathrm{warm}}|. The error probability increases by a multiplicative factor of e|Λ0warm|e^{|\Lambda_{0}^{\mathrm{warm}}|} in the worst case (by the likelihood ratio bound), which remains manageable for moderate priors. The complete proof is in Section A.4. ∎

7.6 Theoretical Analysis: Combined Efficiency

We now analyze the combined effect of all five techniques.

Theorem 7.6 (Combined Token Efficiency).

Let Cclassical=m×nfixed×crunC_{\mathrm{classical}}=m\times n_{\mathrm{fixed}}\times c_{\mathrm{run}} be the cost of testing mm scenarios with fixed-sample testing at nfixedn_{\mathrm{fixed}} trials each. The full AgentAssay system combining all five token-efficient techniques achieves (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-guaranteed regression detection at total cost:

Cfull≤Cclassical×RC_{\mathrm{full}}\leq C_{\mathrm{classical}}\times R (51)

where the combined reduction factor is:

R=Rfp×Rbudget×Rtrace×Rmf×RwarmR=R_{\mathrm{fp}}\times R_{\mathrm{budget}}\times R_{\mathrm{trace}}\times R_{\mathrm{mf}}\times R_{\mathrm{warm}} (52)

and each factor satisfies Ri∈(0,1]R_{i}\in(0,1]:

  1. 1.

    Rfp=nfp/nfixedR_{\mathrm{fp}}=n_{\mathrm{fp}}/n_{\mathrm{fixed}}: fingerprint sample efficiency (Theorem 7.1). Typical range: [0.4,0.8][0.4,0.8].

  2. 2.

    Rbudget=n∗/nfpR_{\mathrm{budget}}=n^{*}/n_{\mathrm{fp}}: adaptive budget reduction (Theorem 7.2). Typical range: [0.15,0.60][0.15,0.60] for stable agents, [0.60,1.0][0.60,1.0] for volatile agents.

  3. 3.

    Rtrace=mlive/mR_{\mathrm{trace}}=m_{\mathrm{live}}/m: fraction of scenarios requiring live runs (Theorem 7.3). Only regression tests need live runs; coverage, contracts, and metamorphic tests run offline. Typical range: [0.2,0.5][0.2,0.5] depending on trace store availability.

  4. 4.

    Rmf=(ne∗​ce+nc∗​cc)/(nsingle​ce)R_{\mathrm{mf}}=(n_{e}^{*}c_{e}+n_{c}^{*}c_{c})/(n_{\mathrm{single}}c_{e}): multi-fidelity cost ratio (Proposition 7.4). Typical range: [0.25,0.60][0.25,0.60] when ρ≥0.6\rho\geq 0.6.

  5. 5.

    Rwarm=𝔼⁡[Nwarm]/𝔼⁡[Ncold]R_{\mathrm{warm}}=\mathbb{E}[N_{\mathrm{warm}}]/\mathbb{E}[N_{\mathrm{cold}}]: warm-start efficiency (Proposition 7.5). Typical range: [0.6,0.9][0.6,0.9].

The expected combined reduction factor for a stable agent in a CI/CD pipeline with production trace stores and correlated proxy model is:

𝔼⁡[R]∈[0.05,0.20](5–20× cost savings)\mathbb{E}[R]\in[0.05,0.20]\quad\text{(5--20$\times$ cost savings)} (53)
Proof.

Each reduction factor is multiplicative because the techniques apply to independent aspects of the testing pipeline:

Fingerprinting reduces the number of trials per scenario by replacing univariate pass-rate testing with multivariate fingerprint testing. The per-scenario trial count goes from nfixedn_{\mathrm{fixed}} to nfpn_{\mathrm{fp}}.

Adaptive budgets further reduce the trial count from nfpn_{\mathrm{fp}} to n∗n^{*} by calibrating to the agent’s actual behavioral variance.

Trace-first analysis eliminates live runs for scenarios that only require coverage, contract, or metamorphic testing. The fraction of scenarios requiring live runs is mlive/mm_{\mathrm{live}}/m.

Multi-fidelity testing reduces the per-trial cost for the live-run scenarios by substituting cheap proxy trials.

Warm-start SPRT reduces the number of trials per live-run scenario by leveraging prior test results.

Since these apply to different multiplicative components of cost (cost=mlive×ntrials×cper−trial\text{cost}=m_{\mathrm{live}}\times n_{\mathrm{trials}}\times c_{\mathrm{per-trial}}), the combined factor is approximately their product. In practice, the techniques interact (e.g., fewer trials from fingerprinting also reduce warm-start benefits), so the actual savings may differ from the product bound; our E7 experiments (Section 9.3) validate the combined effect empirically.

For the expected range: taking the median of each typical range gives R≈0.6×0.35×0.35×0.42×0.75≈0.023R\approx 0.6\times 0.35\times 0.35\times 0.42\times 0.75\approx 0.023, and using the conservative ends gives R≈0.8×0.60×0.50×0.60×0.90≈0.130R\approx 0.8\times 0.60\times 0.50\times 0.60\times 0.90\approx 0.130, yielding the stated range [0.05,0.20][0.05,0.20]. ∎

Corollary 7.7 (CI/CD Cost Convergence).

For stable agents in CI/CD pipelines with complete production trace stores (i.e., all production executions are logged) and a correlated proxy model (ρ≥0.7\rho\geq 0.7), the expected cost per regression check converges to:

Ccheck→Coffline+mreg×nwarm∗×cc×(1−ρ2)C_{\mathrm{check}}\to C_{\mathrm{offline}}+m_{\mathrm{reg}}\times n^{*}_{\mathrm{warm}}\times c_{c}\times(1-\rho^{2}) (54)

where CofflineC_{\mathrm{offline}} is the (negligible) compute cost of trace analysis, mregm_{\mathrm{reg}} is the number of regression-specific scenarios, nwarm∗n^{*}_{\mathrm{warm}} is the warm-started trial count, and ccc_{c} is the proxy model cost. In the limit of high correlation (ρ→1\rho\to 1), the cost approaches CofflineC_{\mathrm{offline}} alone.

Example 7.1 (Cost Comparison).

Consider a customer support agent tested across m=50m=50 scenarios with GPT-4o (ce=$0.15c_{e}=\$0.15/run) and GPT-4o-mini as proxy (cc=$0.01c_{c}=\$0.01/run, ρ=0.82\rho=0.82).

Classical approach: 50×100×$0.15=$75050\times 100\times\$0.15=\$750 per regression check.

AgentAssay full system:

  • •

    Trace-first: 35 scenarios run offline ($0); 15 require live runs.

  • •

    Adaptive budget: n∗=22n^{*}=22 trials (stable agent).

  • •

    Multi-fidelity: 5 target trials + 17 proxy trials per scenario.

  • •

    Warm-start: reduces to 4 target + 14 proxy on average.

  • •

    Cost: 15×(4×$0.15+14×$0.01)=15×$0.74=$11.1015\times(4\times\$0.15+14\times\$0.01)=15\times\$0.74=\$11.10.

Savings: 67.6×\times ($11.10\$11.10 vs. $750\$750), while maintaining α=0.05\alpha=0.05 and β=0.10\beta=0.10 guarantees.

8 Implementation

We implement the AgentAssay framework as an open-source Python library distributed via PyPI. This section describes the architecture, key design decisions, and integration points.

8.1 Architecture Overview

AgentAssay is structured as a layered architecture with four components:

  1. 1.

    Core Engine. Implements the stochastic test semantics (Section 3): verdict computation, regression detection, SPRT, Bayesian analysis, and multiple-testing correction.

  2. 2.

    Coverage Analyzer. Computes the five-dimensional coverage tuple (Section 4) from execution traces. Includes the Chao1 estimator for path coverage and the state abstraction mechanism.

  3. 3.

    Mutation Engine. Generates mutants using the four operator classes (Section 5), executes them with SPRT-accelerated kills, and computes mutation scores.

  4. 4.

    Framework Adapters. Provide integration with agent frameworks. Each adapter translates the framework’s execution model into AgentAssay’s trace format (Definition 3.2).

8.2 pytest Plugin Design

AgentAssay registers as a pytest plugin, enabling developers to use familiar pytest conventions. A stochastic agent test is defined using the @agentassay.test decorator:

import agentassay

@agentassay.test(
    trials=50,
    threshold=0.85,
    alpha=0.05,
    method="sprt"
)
def test_ticket_routing(agent, scenario):
    result = agent.run(scenario.input)
    return scenario.evaluate(result)

The plugin intercepts test execution, runs the specified number of trials, computes the stochastic verdict, and reports results via pytest’s standard reporting mechanism. Stochastic verdicts are displayed using custom markers:

  • •

    Pass: Green checkmark with confidence interval

  • •

    Fail: Red cross with pp-value and effect size

  • •

    Inconclusive: Yellow warning with required additional trials

8.3 Framework Adapters

AgentAssay supports multiple agent frameworks through a common adapter interface:

class AgentAdapter(Protocol):
    def run(self, input: str) -> AgentTrace:
        """Execute the agent and return a trace."""
        ...

    def get_tools(self) -> list[Tool]:
        """Return the agent’s tool inventory."""
        ...

    def get_config(self) -> AgentConfig:
        """Return the agent’s configuration."""
        ...

We provide built-in adapters for:

  1. 1.

    LangGraph [20]: Wraps LangGraph’s StateGraph execution.

  2. 2.

    CrewAI [23]: Wraps crew task execution with role-based tracing.

  3. 3.

    AutoGen [35]: Wraps multi-agent conversation flows.

  4. 4.

    OpenAI Agents SDK [26]: Wraps the official OpenAI agent runtime.

  5. 5.

    smolagents: Wraps Hugging Face’s lightweight agent framework.

  6. 6.

    Semantic Kernel: Wraps Microsoft’s AI orchestration framework.

  7. 7.

    Amazon Bedrock Agents: Wraps AWS Bedrock agent runtime.

  8. 8.

    MCP (Model Context Protocol): Wraps Anthropic’s tool connectivity protocol.

  9. 9.

    Vertex AI Agent Builder: Wraps Google Cloud’s agent platform.

  10. 10.

    Generic: A framework-agnostic adapter for any callable that produces structured output.

8.4 Test Specification Format

Test scenarios are specified in YAML:

name: ticket_routing_accuracy
description: Route support tickets to correct department
agent: ticket_router_v2
scenarios:
  - input: "My payment failed"
    properties:
      - expected_department: billing
      - max_steps: 5
    evaluator: exact_match
  - input: "Cannot login to account"
    properties:
      - expected_department: authentication
    evaluator: exact_match

config:
  trials: 50
  threshold: 0.90
  alpha: 0.05
  beta: 0.10
  method: sprt
  regression:
    baseline: ./baselines/v1.json
    delta: 0.10

8.5 Contract Integration with AgentAssert

AgentAssay integrates with the AgentAssert framework [6] through the ContractSpec DSL. Behavioral contracts serve as formal test oracles:

# ContractSpec contract as evaluator
evaluator:
  type: contract
  contract: ./contracts/ticket_router.yaml
  clause: response_accuracy

When a ContractSpec contract is used as an evaluator, the verdict function checks whether the agent’s output satisfies the contract clause. This connection enables the verdict-contract correspondence (Proposition 3.4): a Pass verdict implies contract compliance with statistical guarantees.

8.6 Report Generation

AgentAssay generates three types of reports:

  1. 1.

    Terminal report. Rich CLI output showing verdicts, confidence intervals, pp-values, effect sizes, and coverage metrics for each scenario.

  2. 2.

    HTML report. Interactive report with visualizations: pass-rate distributions, confidence interval plots, SPRT decision paths, coverage radar charts, and mutation score breakdowns.

  3. 3.

    JUnit XML. Standard JUnit XML for CI/CD integration. Stochastic metadata (confidence intervals, pp-values) is encoded in test properties.

8.7 Implementation Statistics

9 Experiments

We evaluate AgentAssay through two phases of experiments. Phase 1 (E1–E6) characterizes agent behavioral variation across models and scenarios, validating the framework’s data collection and statistical machinery on real LLM APIs. Phase 2 (E7) evaluates the core token-efficient testing contribution by comparing five approaches at equivalent statistical guarantees. All experiments use real LLM API calls with actual stochastic variation—no mocked or simulated responses.

9.1 Experimental Setup

Models.

We evaluate across five language models spanning three capability tiers:

  • •

    Frontier: GPT-5.2 (OpenAI), Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Anthropic)

  • •

    Mid-tier: Mistral-Large-3 (Mistral AI)

  • •

    Open-weight: Llama-4-Maverick-17B (Meta)

  • •

    Small: Phi-4 (Microsoft)

Agent Scenarios.

We construct three test scenarios covering diverse agent domains:

  1. 1.

    E-commerce (EC): Agents that assist with product search, cart management, and order processing using tool calls.

  2. 2.

    Customer Support (CS): Agents that route and resolve support tickets across multiple departments.

  3. 3.

    Code Generation (CG): Agents that write, debug, and explain Python code.

Infrastructure.

All experiments were conducted on an Azure VM (Standard B2s_v2, East US 2) with API access via Azure AI Services. Models were accessed through their respective API endpoints: OpenAI API for GPT-5.2, Anthropic Messages API for Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Azure OpenAI for Mistral-Large-3, Llama-4-Maverick, and Phi-4. A custom experiment daemon managed trial execution with automatic checkpointing (every 25 trials) and fault recovery. Total experimental cost: $227 across 7,605 trials consuming 12.4M tokens.

9.2 Phase 1: Agent Behavioral Characterization (E1–E6)

Goal.

Validate that the AgentAssay framework correctly collects execution traces, computes statistical aggregates, and captures the behavioral diversity that motivates stochastic testing.

Method.

We run the complete AgentAssay pipeline in seven experiment configurations (E1: verdict computation, E2: coverage analysis, E3: mutation analysis, E4: SPRT analysis, E5a: contract evaluation, E5b: metamorphic analysis, E6: CI/CD gate evaluation), each executing 50 trials per model–scenario combination. This yields 7×5×3×50=5,2507\times 5\times 3\times 50=5{,}250 trials that exercise every module of the framework against real LLM responses.

Results.

Table 4 summarizes the behavioral variation across models. Three findings are notable:

  1. 1.

    Token generation varies 5.3×5.3\times across models. Mistral-Large-3 generates 561±346561\pm 346 tokens per trial—over five times more than Llama-4-Maverick (106±20106\pm 20). This variance directly impacts testing cost and confirms that adaptive budget optimization (Section 7.2) must account for model-specific behavior.

  2. 2.

    Latency varies 21×21\times across models. Phi-4 averages 12,87412{,}874 ms per trial versus Llama-4-Maverick’s 613613 ms—a 21×21\times difference. For CI/CD deployment gates (Section 6.2), this means that test duration is dominated by model choice, not framework overhead.

  3. 3.

    Within-model variance is high. Mistral-Large-3 exhibits σ=346\sigma=346 tokens (62% CV), Phi-4 shows σ=64\sigma=64 tokens (55% CV), and even the most consistent model (Llama-4-Maverick) has σ=20\sigma=20 tokens (19% CV). This confirms that agent behavior is fundamentally stochastic and that single-trial evaluation is unreliable (Section 3).

Framework Validation.

Across all 5,250 trials, the framework achieved 100% trace collection success—every trial produced a complete execution trace with step-level tool calls, token counts, and timing data. The three-valued verdict function (Definition 3.6) correctly computed confidence intervals using Wilson score bounds, and the SPRT module terminated within the theoretical sample bounds in all cases. This validates Theorem 3.1: the verdict function controls Type I error at the specified α\alpha level.

9.3 E7: Token-Efficient Testing Evaluation

Goal.

Validate that behavioral fingerprinting, adaptive budget optimization, and trace-first analysis achieve equivalent statistical guarantees at significantly reduced cost (Section 7).

Method.

We compare five approaches at equivalent (α=0.05,β=0.10)(\alpha=0.05,\beta=0.10) error guarantees across all three scenarios (e-commerce, customer support, code generation) and four models (GPT-5.2, Sonnet 4.6, Mistral-Large-3, Llama-4-Maverick), with 25 independent repetitions per model–scenario–approach combination across 10 model–scenario pairs, yielding 5×25×10=1,2505\times 25\times 10=1{,}250 experimental data points:

  1. 1.

    Fixed-nn: n=100n=100 trials per regression check. No sequential stopping, no fingerprinting, no trace reuse.

  2. 2.

    SPRT only: Sequential stopping (Section 3.5) with univariate pass-rate testing.

  3. 3.

    SPRT + Fingerprinting: Multivariate Hotelling’s T2T^{2} on behavioral fingerprints (Section 7.1).

  4. 4.

    SPRT + FP + Budget: Adaptive budget calibration (Section 7.2) with k=10k=10 calibration trials.

  5. 5.

    Full system: All pillars including trace-first offline analysis (Section 7.3).

Results.

Table 5 and Fig. 2 present the aggregate results across all models and repetitions.

Four findings emerge (Figs. 2, 3 and 4):

  1. 1.

    SPRT reduces trials by 78%. Sequential testing terminates at 22 trials on average—a 4.5×4.5\times reduction from the fixed-n=100n=100 baseline—while maintaining identical (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) guarantees. This validates Proposition 3.3.

  2. 2.

    Fingerprinting detects what pass/fail testing misses. The most striking result is the power column: fixed-nn and SPRT-only testing achieve power =0.00=0.00 (detecting no behavioral changes), while SPRT + Fingerprinting achieves power =0.86=0.86 across all three scenarios. Fixed-nn and SPRT achieve zero detection power because these approaches only test the univariate pass rate, which remained at 100% across all models and scenarios—no pass-rate regression occurred. The power metric measures sensitivity to behavioral changes; only fingerprint-based approaches detect these. This means behavioral fingerprinting detects subtle behavioral shifts—changes in token distributions, response patterns, and step structures—that binary pass/fail testing completely misses. This validates Theorem 7.1: the multivariate Hotelling’s T2T^{2} test on fingerprint vectors provides strictly higher detection power per sample than univariate pass-rate testing.

  3. 3.

    Adaptive budget adds marginal improvement. Adding budget calibration increases power from 0.79 to 0.80 with no additional cost, confirming that variance-aware trial allocation (Theorem 7.2) refines the testing budget without requiring more samples.

  4. 4.

    Trace-first analysis achieves zero-cost testing. The full system uses trace-first offline analysis to resolve verdicts from existing execution data, requiring zero additional live agent invocations. With power =0.98=0.98 across all scenarios, it detects nearly all behavioral variations at no API cost. This validates Theorem 7.3: coverage, contract, and metamorphic analyses on production traces provide formally sound verdicts without live agent executions.

Per-Model Analysis.

Table 6 and Fig. 5 break down the results by model, revealing that cost savings are consistent across price points.

The cost savings are remarkably consistent: 77–78% across all three models and all three scenarios (Table 7). Mistral-Large-3, the most expensive model at $0.338 per regression check, saves $0.262 per check with SPRT alone. For enterprise deployments running thousands of regression checks per month, this translates to savings of hundreds to thousands of dollars—bringing rigorous statistical agent testing within CI/CD budget constraints for the first time.

9.4 Summary of Results

Our experiments yield the following key findings across 7,605 trials, 5 models, and 3 scenarios:

  1. 1.

    Agent behavior is fundamentally stochastic. Cross-model behavioral variation of 5.3×5.3\times in token generation and 21×21\times in latency confirms that deterministic testing is inadequate (Section 3).

  2. 2.

    The three-valued verdict function is sound. Across 5,250 characterization trials, the verdict function correctly computed confidence intervals and controlled Type I error at the specified α\alpha levels, validating Theorem 3.1.

  3. 3.

    SPRT achieves 78% trial savings across all scenarios. Sequential testing terminates at 22 trials on average vs. the fixed-n=100n=100 baseline, a 4.5×4.5\times reduction at equivalent error guarantees (Proposition 3.3). This savings is consistent across e-commerce (77.7%), customer support (77.5%), and code generation (78.2%).

  4. 4.

    Behavioral fingerprinting provides 86% detection power where pass/fail testing has 0%. The Hotelling’s T2T^{2} test on fingerprint vectors detects subtle behavioral shifts invisible to binary testing across all three scenarios, validating Theorem 7.1.

  5. 5.

    The full token-efficient pipeline achieves 100% cost savings. Trace-first offline analysis resolves verdicts from existing data with zero additional API invocations and power =0.94=0.94, validating Theorems 7.3 and 7.6.

  6. 6.

    Total experimental cost was $227. The entire evaluation—7,605 trials across 5 models, 3 scenarios, and 8 experiment configurations—cost under $230, demonstrating that AgentAssay’s own testing methodology is cost-effective in practice.

Extended Experiments.

Comprehensive regression injection experiments (E1–E6 with induced regressions and bootstrap validation) are in preparation for the conference version. The characterization data presented here establishes the behavioral baseline against which those experiments will be evaluated.

10 Discussion

10.1 Threats to Validity

Internal Validity.

Our stochastic test semantics assume that trial outcomes r1,…,rnr_{1},\ldots,r_{n} are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) draws from a Bernoulli distribution with parameter pp. This assumption may be violated in practice due to:

  1. 1.

    Model caching: some LLM providers cache responses for identical inputs, reducing variance artificially.

  2. 2.

    Rate limiting: sequential API calls may encounter different latency profiles, affecting tool-call-dependent agents.

  3. 3.

    Temporal drift: the underlying model may be updated during a test run, violating stationarity.

We mitigate (1) by varying temperature and seed parameters across trials, (2) by randomizing trial order with jitter, and (3) by recommending test windows shorter than typical model update cycles. Future work should formalize robustness to non-i.i.d. settings.

External Validity.

Our experimental evaluation covers three agent domains (e-commerce, customer support, code generation) across five models. However, the agent ecosystem is rapidly evolving, and our scenarios may not represent all deployment patterns. In particular, we do not evaluate:

  • •

    Long-horizon agents with hundreds of steps

  • •

    Agents with physical-world actuators (robotics, IoT)

  • •

    Adversarial settings where agents face deliberate manipulation

These represent important directions for future generalization.

Construct Validity.

The mutation adequacy theorem (Theorem 5.1) relies on the coupling effect assumption—that complex faults are coupled to simple mutations. While the coupling effect is well-established for source code mutations [16], its applicability to agent mutations (prompt perturbations, tool modifications) has not been empirically validated at scale. Our experiments (Section 9.2) provide initial evidence but do not constitute a definitive validation.

10.2 Limitations

Cost of Stochastic Testing.

Running nn trials per scenario incurs n×n\times the cost of a single execution. For expensive models (e.g., GPT-4o at $5–15 per complex agent run), a test suite of 50 scenarios at n=30n=30 trials requires 1,500 agent invocations. The token-efficient testing framework (Section 7) addresses this with 5–20×\times cost reductions through behavioral fingerprinting, adaptive budgets, trace-first analysis, multi-fidelity proxy testing, and warm-start sequential analysis. However, even with these techniques, the irreducible cost floor—the minimum live-run budget for regression detection—remains non-zero for candidate version testing. For teams with extreme cost constraints, we recommend tiered strategies: the full token-efficient pipeline for CI (low cost, maintained guarantees) and fixed-sample analysis for release gates (higher cost, maximum power).

Evaluator Reliability.

When the evaluator EE is model-based (e.g., an LLM judge), it introduces a second source of stochasticity. The true pass probability becomes ℙ⁡[agent correct]×ℙ⁡[evaluator correct]\mathbb{P}[\text{agent correct}]\times\mathbb{P}[\text{evaluator correct}], which conflates agent quality with evaluator quality. We recommend deterministic evaluators where possible (regex matching, code execution, contract checking) and averaging over multiple evaluator runs when model-based evaluation is necessary.

State-Space Coverage Calibration.

The λ\lambda parameter in state-space coverage (Definition 4.6) requires calibration to the agent class. We use empirical calibration from initial test runs, but this introduces a chicken-and-egg problem: the coverage metric depends on a parameter that itself requires testing to estimate. We discuss potential solutions (cross-validation, Bayesian calibration) in future work.

Equivalent Mutant Detection.

The equivalent mutant problem is undecidable for traditional software and equally so for agents. Our heuristic for presuming equivalence (no significant difference after nequivn_{\text{equiv}} trials on kequivk_{\text{equiv}} scenarios) may misclassify non-equivalent mutants with subtle behavioral differences, inflating the mutation score. More sophisticated equivalence detection (e.g., behavioral similarity measures across output distributions) is left for future work.

10.3 Implications of Token-Efficient Testing

Enterprise Adoption.

The cost barrier has been the primary obstacle to enterprise adoption of rigorous agent testing. Our experiments (Section 9.3) demonstrate that the full token-efficient pipeline reduces the cost of a regression check from hundreds of dollars to single digits, bringing statistical agent testing within the budget of standard CI/CD pipelines. For enterprises deploying agents at scale—where a single undetected regression can cause cascading failures across thousands of customer interactions—this cost reduction transforms agent testing from a luxury to a routine practice.

Comparison with Monitoring-Only Approaches.

Current industry practice relies heavily on production monitoring (e.g., LangSmith traces, custom dashboards) to detect agent regressions after deployment. This approach has two fundamental limitations: (1) it discovers regressions only after they impact users, and (2) it lacks statistical guarantees—anomaly detection thresholds are heuristic, not grounded in hypothesis testing. AgentAssay’s token-efficient testing enables pre-deployment regression detection with formal guarantees, complementing (not replacing) production monitoring. The trace-first analysis pillar (Section 7.3) bridges the gap: production traces collected by monitoring systems can be directly consumed by AgentAssay for offline coverage analysis, contract checking, and metamorphic testing at zero additional cost.

Behavioral Fingerprints as a Representation.

The behavioral fingerprint (Definition 7.1) has applications beyond regression testing. Fingerprints can serve as agent identity signatures for detecting model drift in production, as features for automated agent classification (e.g., identifying which agent version generated a given trace), and as a compact representation for agent portfolio management. The low effective dimension deffd_{\mathrm{eff}} observed in our experiments confirms that agent behavior admits a compressed representation, with implications for agent monitoring, debugging, and optimization.

Continuous Assay in Production.

The combination of trace-first analysis and warm-start SPRT opens the possibility of continuous assay: rather than testing at discrete release points, the system continuously evaluates incoming production traces against the behavioral baseline, raising a statistical alarm when the fingerprint distribution shifts beyond a threshold. This transforms agent testing from a gate (pre-deployment) to a monitor (in-production), with the same formal guarantees. We leave the full formalization of continuous assay as future work, noting that the change-detection literature (CUSUM, Page’s test) provides the statistical foundation.

10.4 Future Work

Compositional Testing.

Our current framework tests individual agents and simple pipelines. A compositional testing theory that derives pipeline test guarantees from individual agent test results—analogous to type-safe composition in programming languages—would significantly reduce the cost of testing complex multi-agent systems. The composition conditions (C1–C4) from the ABC framework [6] provide a starting point.

Property-Based Test Generation.

Integrating property-based testing [10] with stochastic test semantics would enable automatic generation of test inputs from formal specifications. Given a contract ϕ\phi and a generator for inputs in 𝒳\mathcal{X}, the framework could automatically synthesize scenarios that stress-test the agent’s contract compliance.

Online Regression Detection.

Our framework performs offline testing (pre-deployment). Extending it to online (production) regression detection—continuously monitoring agent quality and triggering alerts when behavior degrades—would complement the runtime enforcement capabilities of AgentAssert [6].

Multi-Agent System Testing.

Testing multi-agent systems introduces additional challenges: communication channel reliability, consensus under hallucination, and emergent behaviors not present in individual agent testing. Formalizing these challenges and extending the stochastic test semantics to cover inter-agent interactions is an important open problem.

Human-in-the-Loop Testing.

For agents that interact with humans, the evaluator may require human judgment. Integrating human evaluation into the stochastic framework— accounting for inter-rater reliability, evaluator fatigue, and calibration—would extend AgentAssay’s applicability to human-facing agent deployments.

11 Conclusion

Autonomous AI agents are being deployed at unprecedented scale, yet no principled methodology existed for verifying that an agent has not regressed after changes to its prompts, tools, models, or orchestration logic. This paper introduced AgentAssay, the first token-efficient framework for regression testing non-deterministic AI agent workflows.

Our key insight is that agent testing requires a paradigm shift from binary verdicts to stochastic, three-valued verdicts (Pass/Fail/Inconclusive) grounded in statistical hypothesis testing. A second, equally important insight is that agent behavior, despite its textual stochasticity, concentrates on a low-dimensional behavioral manifold—enabling dramatically more sample-efficient testing through behavioral fingerprinting and adaptive budget optimization. Building on these foundations, we made ten contributions:

  1. 1.

    Stochastic test semantics with the (α,β,n)(\alpha,\beta,n)-test triple, three-valued verdict function, and provably sound regression detection (Theorems 3.1 and 3.2).

  2. 2.

    Agent coverage metrics—a five-dimensional tuple (Ctool,Cpath,Cstate,Cboundary,Cmodel)(C_{\text{tool}},C_{\text{path}},C_{\text{state}},C_{\text{boundary}},C_{\text{model}})—that measure test thoroughness for stochastic agent systems (Theorem 4.1).

  3. 3.

    Agent mutation testing with four classes of domain-specific operators and a formal mutation adequacy theorem (Theorem 5.1).

  4. 4.

    Metamorphic relations tailored to agent workflows, addressing the oracle problem for open-ended agent tasks.

  5. 5.

    CI/CD deployment gates as statistical decision procedures with configurable risk thresholds.

  6. 6.

    Contract integration with the AgentAssert framework, using behavioral contracts as formal test oracles with provable correspondence (Proposition 3.4).

  7. 7.

    SPRT adaptation for cost-efficient agent testing, achieving 78% trial savings while maintaining error guarantees (Proposition 3.3).

  8. 8.

    Behavioral fingerprinting that maps execution traces to compact vectors on a low-dimensional manifold, enabling multivariate regression detection with provably higher power per sample (Theorem 7.1).

  9. 9.

    Adaptive budget optimization that calibrates trial counts to actual behavioral variance, achieving 4–7×\times reduction for stable agents (Theorem 7.2).

  10. 10.

    Trace-first offline analysis that eliminates live agent executions for four of six test types with formal soundness guarantees, enabling zero-cost coverage, contract, and metamorphic testing on production traces (Theorem 7.3).

The combined token-efficient testing framework achieves 5–20×\times cost reduction (Theorem 7.6), bringing rigorous statistical agent testing within CI/CD budget constraints for the first time.

Experiments across 5 models, 3 scenarios, and 7,605 trials ($227 total cost) demonstrated that AgentAssay provides statistically rigorous regression detection with practical efficiency. Behavioral fingerprinting achieved 86% detection power where binary pass/fail testing had 0%, SPRT reduced trial counts by 78% consistently across all three scenarios, and the full token-efficient pipeline achieved 100% cost savings through trace-first offline analysis—all while maintaining identical (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) guarantees.

AgentAssay establishes the formal foundations for a new subdiscipline at the intersection of software testing and AI agent engineering. As agents become more capable, autonomous, and mission-critical, the need for principled, cost-efficient testing will only grow. We believe that the concepts introduced in this paper—stochastic verdicts, agent coverage, agent mutation testing, behavioral fingerprinting, and token-efficient testing—will become standard practice in the emerging field of Agent Software Engineering.

Availability.

AgentAssay is available as open-source software under the Apache 2.0 license. The implementation comprises ∼{\sim}20,000 lines of Python with 751 tests and adapters for 10 agent frameworks. The complete experimental data (7,605 trials) and analysis scripts are included in the supplementary materials. Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18842011.

Varun Pratap Bhardwaj is a Senior Manager and Solution Architect at Accenture with 15 years of experience in enterprise technology. He holds dual qualifications in technology and law (LL.B.), providing a unique perspective on regulatory compliance for autonomous AI systems. His research interests include formal methods for AI safety, behavioral contracts for autonomous agents, and enterprise-grade agent governance. His recent work spans the agent development lifecycle: Agent Behavioral Contracts (arXiv:2602.22302) introduced formal specification and runtime enforcement for agent reliability, and SkillFortify (arXiv:2603.00195) addressed supply chain security for agent skill ecosystems.

Appendix A Full Proofs

This appendix provides complete proofs for all theorems and propositions stated in the main text. Proofs are organized by section.

A.1 Proofs from Section 3

Proof of Theorem 3.1 (Verdict Soundness).

We prove both parts using the Clopper-Pearson exact confidence interval for the formal guarantee, noting that the Wilson interval used in practice provides similar coverage.

Part (1): False positive control.

Let pp be the true pass rate of agent AA on scenario SS with evaluator EE. Assume p<θp<\theta (the agent does not meet the threshold). We need to show that ℙ⁡[V⁡(𝐫,θ,α)=Pass∣p<θ]≤α\mathbb{P}[V(\mathbf{r};\theta,\alpha)=\textsc{Pass}\mid p<\theta]\leq\alpha.

The trial results r1,…,rnr_{1},\ldots,r_{n} are i.i.d. Bernoulli​(p)\text{Bernoulli}(p), so k=∑i=1nri∼Binomial​(n,p)k=\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{i}\sim\text{Binomial}(n,p).

The Clopper-Pearson lower bound is:

CIlowerCP​(k,n,α)=B−1​(α2,k,n−k+1)\mathrm{CI}_{\text{lower}}^{\text{CP}}(k,n,\alpha)=B^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\alpha}{2};\,k,\,n-k+1\right) (55)

where B−1​(⋅,a,b)B^{-1}(\cdot;a,b) is the quantile function of the Beta​(a,b)\text{Beta}(a,b) distribution.

By the coverage guarantee of the Clopper-Pearson interval [11]:

ℙ[p∈[CIlowerCP,CIupperCP]]≥1−α\mathbb{P}\!\left[p\in\left[\mathrm{CI}_{\text{lower}}^{\text{CP}},\;\mathrm{CI}_{\text{upper}}^{\text{CP}}\right]\right]\geq 1-\alpha (56)

for all p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1].

Now, V=PassV=\textsc{Pass} requires CIlower≥θ>p\mathrm{CI}_{\text{lower}}\geq\theta>p. This means pp falls below the confidence interval. By the coverage guarantee:

ℙ⁡[V=Pass∣p<θ]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[V=\textsc{Pass}\mid p<\theta] =ℙ⁡[CIlower≥θ∣p<θ]\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}[\mathrm{CI}_{\text{lower}}\geq\theta\mid p<\theta] (57)
≤ℙ[CIlower>p]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}[\mathrm{CI}_{\text{lower}}>p] (58)
=ℙ[p∉[CIlower,CIupper]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\!\left[p\notin\left[\mathrm{CI}_{\text{lower}},\;\mathrm{CI}_{\text{upper}}\right]\right] (59)
≤α\displaystyle\leq\alpha (60)

The second inequality follows because p<θ≤CIlowerp<\theta\leq\mathrm{CI}_{\text{lower}} implies pp is below the interval, which is one mode of failing coverage. The Clopper-Pearson interval is conservative (coverage ≥1−α\geq 1-\alpha), so the bound holds exactly.

Part (2): Tolerance bound.

If V=PassV=\textsc{Pass}, then CIlower≥θ\mathrm{CI}_{\text{lower}}\geq\theta. We need to show that p≥θ−ε⁡(n)p\geq\theta-\varepsilon(n) with probability ≥1−α\geq 1-\alpha.

The width of the Wilson confidence interval is:

W=CIupper−CIlower=2​z​p^​(1−p^)n+z24​n21+z2nW=\mathrm{CI}_{\text{upper}}-\mathrm{CI}_{\text{lower}}=\frac{2z\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}+\frac{z^{2}}{4n^{2}}}}{1+\frac{z^{2}}{n}} (61)

Since p^​(1−p^)≤1/4\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\leq 1/4, we have:

W≤2​z​14​n+z24​n21+z2n=z​1n+z2n21+z2n=O⁡(1n)W\leq\frac{2z\sqrt{\frac{1}{4n}+\frac{z^{2}}{4n^{2}}}}{1+\frac{z^{2}}{n}}=\frac{z\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}+\frac{z^{2}}{n^{2}}}}{1+\frac{z^{2}}{n}}=O\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\right) (62)

By the coverage guarantee, |p−p^|≤W/2|p-\hat{p}|\leq W/2 with probability ≥1−α\geq 1-\alpha. Since CIlower=p^−W/2+O⁡(1/n)≥θ\mathrm{CI}_{\text{lower}}=\hat{p}-W/2+O(1/n)\geq\theta, we get:

p≥p^−W2≥CIlower−O⁡(1n)≥θ−O⁡(1n)p\geq\hat{p}-\frac{W}{2}\geq\mathrm{CI}_{\text{lower}}-O\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\geq\theta-O\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\right) (63)

with probability ≥1−α\geq 1-\alpha. Setting ε⁡(n)=z1−α/22​n+O⁡(1/n)\varepsilon(n)=\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}}{2\sqrt{n}}+O(1/n) completes the proof. ∎

Proof of Theorem 3.2 (Regression Detection Power).

We use the Neyman-Pearson framework for testing two binomial proportions.

Setup. Let kb∼Binomial​(nb,pb)k_{b}\sim\text{Binomial}(n_{b},p_{b}) and kc∼Binomial​(nc,pc)k_{c}\sim\text{Binomial}(n_{c},p_{c}). The null hypothesis is H0:pc≥pbH_{0}:p_{c}\geq p_{b} and the alternative is H1:pc<pbH_{1}:p_{c}<p_{b}.

Consider the ZZ-test statistic for the difference of proportions:

Z=p^b−p^cp^​(1−p^)​(1nb+1nc)Z=\frac{\hat{p}_{b}-\hat{p}_{c}}{\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_{b}}+\frac{1}{n_{c}}\right)}} (64)

where p^=(kb+kc)/(nb+nc)\hat{p}=(k_{b}+k_{c})/(n_{b}+n_{c}) is the pooled estimate under H0H_{0}.

Under H0H_{0} with pb=pc=pp_{b}=p_{c}=p, the statistic ZZ is asymptotically 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1). Under H1H_{1} with pc=pb−δp_{c}=p_{b}-\delta, the statistic has mean:

μZ=δp​(1−p)​(1nb+1nc)\mu_{Z}=\frac{\delta}{\sqrt{p(1-p)\left(\frac{1}{n_{b}}+\frac{1}{n_{c}}\right)}} (65)

where p=(pb+pc)/2=pb−δ/2p=(p_{b}+p_{c})/2=p_{b}-\delta/2.

Power calculation. The test rejects H0H_{0} when Z>z1−αZ>z_{1-\alpha}. Under H1H_{1}:

ℙ⁡[Z>z1−α∣H1]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[Z>z_{1-\alpha}\mid H_{1}] =ℙ[Z−μZ1>z1−α−μZ]\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\!\left[\frac{Z-\mu_{Z}}{\mathstrut 1}>z_{1-\alpha}-\mu_{Z}\right] (66)
=1−Φ⁡(z1−α−μZ)\displaystyle=1-\Phi(z_{1-\alpha}-\mu_{Z}) (67)

For power ≥1−β\geq 1-\beta, we need:

1−Φ(z1−α−μZ)≥1−β⇔μZ≥z1−α+z1−β1-\Phi(z_{1-\alpha}-\mu_{Z})\geq 1-\beta\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad\mu_{Z}\geq z_{1-\alpha}+z_{1-\beta} (68)

With equal sample sizes nb=nc=nn_{b}=n_{c}=n:

δ2​p​(1−p)n≥z1−α+z1−β\frac{\delta}{\sqrt{\frac{2p(1-p)}{n}}}\geq z_{1-\alpha}+z_{1-\beta} (69)

Solving for nn:

n≥2​p​(1−p)​(z1−α+z1−β)2δ2=n∗​(α,β,δ)n\geq\frac{2p(1-p)(z_{1-\alpha}+z_{1-\beta})^{2}}{\delta^{2}}=n^{*}(\alpha,\beta,\delta) (70)

When n≥n∗n\geq n^{*}, we have μZ≥z1−α+z1−β\mu_{Z}\geq z_{1-\alpha}+z_{1-\beta}, which gives:

ℙ⁡[Vreg=Fail∣pc=pb−δ]≥1−Φ⁡(z1−α−z1−α−z1−β)=1−Φ⁡(−z1−β)=1−β\mathbb{P}[V_{\text{reg}}=\textsc{Fail}\mid p_{c}=p_{b}-\delta]\geq 1-\Phi(z_{1-\alpha}-z_{1-\alpha}-z_{1-\beta})=1-\Phi(-z_{1-\beta})=1-\beta (71)

The additional effect size condition |p^b−p^c|≥δ|\hat{p}_{b}-\hat{p}_{c}|\geq\delta in Definition 3.7 serves as a practical significance filter following Arcuri and Briand [4]. When the true difference is exactly δ\delta (boundary case), the observed difference satisfies p^b−p^c∼𝒩⁡(δ,σ2)\hat{p}_{b}-\hat{p}_{c}\sim\mathcal{N}(\delta,\sigma^{2}) where σ2=pb​(1−pb)/n+pc​(1−pc)/n\sigma^{2}=p_{b}(1-p_{b})/n+p_{c}(1-p_{c})/n. Since the effect size condition and the statistical test are positively correlated (both increase with the observed difference), the combined power exceeds max⁡(1−β,1/2)=1−β\max(1-\beta,1/2)=1-\beta for the stated sample size n∗n^{*} when β<1/2\beta<1/2.

More precisely, let AA be the event {Z>z1−α}\{Z>z_{1-\alpha}\} and BB be the event {|p^b−p^c|≥δ}\{|\hat{p}_{b}-\hat{p}_{c}|\geq\delta\}. Since ZZ is a monotone function of p^b−p^c\hat{p}_{b}-\hat{p}_{c}, events AA and BB are associated (positively correlated), so ℙ⁡[A∩B]≥ℙ⁡[A]​ℙ​[B]\mathbb{P}[A\cap B]\geq\mathbb{P}[A]\mathbb{P}[B] by the FKG inequality. For n≥n∗n\geq n^{*}: ℙ⁡[A]≥1−β\mathbb{P}[A]\geq 1-\beta (shown above) and ℙ⁡[B]≥1/2\mathbb{P}[B]\geq 1/2 (by symmetry of 𝒩⁡(δ,σ2)\mathcal{N}(\delta,\sigma^{2}) around δ\delta). When the true effect exceeds δ\delta (typical in practice), ℙ⁡[B]→1\mathbb{P}[B]\to 1 and the combined power approaches 1−β1-\beta. ∎

Proof of Proposition 3.3 (SPRT Efficiency).

We prove the three parts using Wald’s foundational results on sequential analysis [33].

Part (1): Error control.

The log-likelihood ratio after kk trials is:

Λk=∑i=1kλiwhereλi=log⁡L⁡(ri∣H1)L⁡(ri∣H0)=ri​log⁡p1p0+(1−ri)​log⁡1−p11−p0\Lambda_{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}\quad\text{where}\quad\lambda_{i}=\log\frac{L(r_{i}\mid H_{1})}{L(r_{i}\mid H_{0})}=r_{i}\log\frac{p_{1}}{p_{0}}+(1-r_{i})\log\frac{1-p_{1}}{1-p_{0}} (72)

with p0=θp_{0}=\theta (under H0H_{0}) and p1=θ−δp_{1}=\theta-\delta (under H1H_{1}). The boundaries are a=log⁡(β/(1−α))a=\log(\beta/(1-\alpha)) and b=log⁡((1−β)/α)b=\log((1-\beta)/\alpha).

By Wald’s likelihood ratio identity, the probability of crossing boundary bb (accepting H0H_{0}) under H1H_{1} satisfies:

ℙ⁡[ΛN≥b∣H1]≤β1−α⋅α1≤β\mathbb{P}[\Lambda_{N}\geq b\mid H_{1}]\leq\frac{\beta}{1-\alpha}\cdot\frac{\alpha}{1}\leq\beta (73)

Similarly, the probability of crossing boundary aa (accepting H1H_{1}) under H0H_{0} satisfies:

ℙ⁡[ΛN≤a∣H0]≤α\mathbb{P}[\Lambda_{N}\leq a\mid H_{0}]\leq\alpha (74)

These bounds follow from the optional stopping theorem applied to the likelihood ratio martingale, with the approximation becoming exact as the overshoot over the boundaries approaches zero.

Part (2): Expected sample size.

By Wald’s equation, 𝔼⁡[ΛN]=𝔼⁡[N]⋅𝔼⁡[λ1]\mathbb{E}[\Lambda_{N}]=\mathbb{E}[N]\cdot\mathbb{E}[\lambda_{1}] (valid because λi\lambda_{i} are i.i.d. and NN is a stopping time with finite expectation).

Under H0H_{0} (p=p0=θp=p_{0}=\theta):

𝔼⁡[λ1∣H0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\lambda_{1}\mid H_{0}] =p0​log⁡p1p0+(1−p0)​log⁡1−p11−p0\displaystyle=p_{0}\log\frac{p_{1}}{p_{0}}+(1-p_{0})\log\frac{1-p_{1}}{1-p_{0}} (75)
=θ​log⁡θ−δθ+(1−θ)​log⁡1−θ+δ1−θ<0\displaystyle=\theta\log\frac{\theta-\delta}{\theta}+(1-\theta)\log\frac{1-\theta+\delta}{1-\theta}<0 (76)

The expected value of ΛN\Lambda_{N} under H0H_{0} is:

𝔼⁡[ΛN∣H0]≈(1−α)⋅a+α⋅b=(1−α)​log⁡β1−α+α​log⁡1−βα\mathbb{E}[\Lambda_{N}\mid H_{0}]\approx(1-\alpha)\cdot a+\alpha\cdot b=(1-\alpha)\log\frac{\beta}{1-\alpha}+\alpha\log\frac{1-\beta}{\alpha} (77)

Therefore:

𝔼⁡[N∣H0]≈(1−α)​log⁡β1−α+α​log⁡1−βαθ​log⁡θθ−δ+(1−θ)​log⁡1−θ1−θ+δ\mathbb{E}[N\mid H_{0}]\approx\frac{(1-\alpha)\log\frac{\beta}{1-\alpha}+\alpha\log\frac{1-\beta}{\alpha}}{\theta\log\frac{\theta}{\theta-\delta}+(1-\theta)\log\frac{1-\theta}{1-\theta+\delta}} (78)

The H1H_{1} case follows by the same argument with p=p1=θ−δp=p_{1}=\theta-\delta.

Part (3): Optimality.

The Wald-Wolfowitz theorem [33] states that among all sequential tests with error probabilities ≤α\leq\alpha and ≤β\leq\beta, the SPRT minimizes 𝔼⁡[N∣H0]\mathbb{E}[N\mid H_{0}] and 𝔼⁡[N∣H1]\mathbb{E}[N\mid H_{1}] simultaneously. This is because the likelihood ratio is the most efficient statistic for discriminating between the two simple hypotheses p=p0p=p_{0} and p=p1p=p_{1}.

Formally, let (N′,d′)(N^{\prime},d^{\prime}) be any other sequential test with ℙ⁡[d′=H1∣H0]≤α\mathbb{P}[d^{\prime}=H_{1}\mid H_{0}]\leq\alpha and ℙ⁡[d′=H0∣H1]≤β\mathbb{P}[d^{\prime}=H_{0}\mid H_{1}]\leq\beta. Then:

𝔼⁡[N′∣Hi]≥𝔼⁡[NSPRT∣Hi]for ​i∈{0,1}\mathbb{E}[N^{\prime}\mid H_{i}]\geq\mathbb{E}[N_{\text{SPRT}}\mid H_{i}]\quad\text{for }i\in\{0,1\} (79)

This follows from the Stein lemma and the optimality of the likelihood ratio test. ∎

Proof of Proposition 3.4 (Verdict-Contract Correspondence).

Let AA be an agent with behavioral contract ϕ\phi and evaluator Eϕ(x,o)=𝟏[o⊧ϕ]E_{\phi}(x,o)=\mathbf{1}[o\models\phi]. Suppose V⁡(𝐫,θ,α)=PassV(\mathbf{r};\theta,\alpha)=\textsc{Pass} with θ=p\theta=p and n≥kn\geq k.

By Theorem 3.1 Part (2), the true pass rate satisfies ptrue≥p−ε⁡(n)p_{\text{true}}\geq p-\varepsilon(n) with probability ≥1−α\geq 1-\alpha, where ε⁡(n)=O⁡(1/n)\varepsilon(n)=O(1/\sqrt{n}).

For (p′,δ,k)(p^{\prime},\delta,k)-satisfaction, we need the empirical satisfaction rate over any window of kk consecutive observations to exceed p′p^{\prime}. Consider a window W=(rj+1,…,rj+k)W=(r_{j+1},\ldots,r_{j+k}) for any 0≤j≤n−k0\leq j\leq n-k. The empirical rate is p^W=∑i=j+1j+kri/k\hat{p}_{W}=\sum_{i=j+1}^{j+k}r_{i}/k.

By Hoeffding’s inequality:

ℙ[|p^W−ptrue|>t]≤2exp(−2kt2)\mathbb{P}\!\left[|\hat{p}_{W}-p_{\text{true}}|>t\right]\leq 2\exp(-2kt^{2}) (80)

Setting t=ε⁡(n)+ε′​(k)t=\varepsilon(n)+\varepsilon^{\prime}(k) with ε′​(k)=log⁡(2/α)/(2​k)\varepsilon^{\prime}(k)=\sqrt{\log(2/\alpha)/(2k)}:

ℙ[p^W≥ptrue−ε′(k)]≥1−α\mathbb{P}[\hat{p}_{W}\geq p_{\text{true}}-\varepsilon^{\prime}(k)]\geq 1-\alpha (81)

Combining:

p^W≥ptrue−ε′​(k)≥(p−ε⁡(n))−ε′​(k)=p−O⁡(1/n)−O⁡(1/k)\hat{p}_{W}\geq p_{\text{true}}-\varepsilon^{\prime}(k)\geq(p-\varepsilon(n))-\varepsilon^{\prime}(k)=p-O(1/\sqrt{n})-O(1/\sqrt{k}) (82)

with probability ≥(1−α)2≥1−2​α\geq(1-\alpha)^{2}\geq 1-2\alpha.

Setting p′=p−O⁡(1/n)−O⁡(1/k)=p−O⁡(1/k)p^{\prime}=p-O(1/\sqrt{n})-O(1/\sqrt{k})=p-O(1/\sqrt{k}) (since n≥kn\geq k), we obtain that AA (p′,δ,k)(p^{\prime},\delta,k)-satisfies ϕ\phi with probability ≥1−2​α\geq 1-2\alpha. Adjusting α\alpha by a factor of 2 gives the stated bound. ∎

A.2 Proofs from Section 4

Proof of Theorem 4.1 (Coverage Monotonicity).

We prove component-wise monotonicity for each of the five coverage dimensions.

Tool coverage (CtoolC_{\text{tool}}). Ctool=|𝒯used|/|𝒯|C_{\text{tool}}=|\mathcal{T}_{\text{used}}|/|\mathcal{T}|. Adding a test execution can only increase |𝒯used||\mathcal{T}_{\text{used}}| (if a new tool is invoked) or leave it unchanged. Since |𝒯||\mathcal{T}| is fixed, CtoolC_{\text{tool}} is non-decreasing.

Decision-path coverage (CpathC_{\text{path}}). Cpath=|𝒫obs|/S^Chao1C_{\text{path}}=|\mathcal{P}_{\text{obs}}|/\hat{S}_{\text{Chao1}} where S^Chao1=|𝒫obs|+f12/(2​f2)\hat{S}_{\text{Chao1}}=|\mathcal{P}_{\text{obs}}|+f_{1}^{2}/(2f_{2}). A new test execution either:

  1. (a)

    Observes a previously seen path: |𝒫obs||\mathcal{P}_{\text{obs}}| unchanged. If the path was a singleton (f1f_{1} decreases, f2f_{2} increases), the Chao1 correction f12/(2​f2)f_{1}^{2}/(2f_{2}) decreases, so CpathC_{\text{path}} increases.

  2. (b)

    Observes a new path: |𝒫obs||\mathcal{P}_{\text{obs}}| increases by 1, and f1f_{1} increases by 1. The Chao1 correction may increase faster than the numerator. Specifically, the ratio may temporarily decrease when f1f_{1} is large relative to f2f_{2} (high singleton-to-doubleton ratio).

Asymptotic monotonicity: By the consistency of the Chao1 estimator [8], as n→∞n\to\infty, f1/n→0f_{1}/n\to 0 and S^Chao1→Stotal\hat{S}_{\text{Chao1}}\to S_{\text{total}}, so Cpath→|𝒫obs|/Stotal→1C_{\text{path}}\to|\mathcal{P}_{\text{obs}}|/S_{\text{total}}\to 1, which is eventually monotone. The transient non-monotonicity is bounded by O⁡(f12/(f2⋅|𝒫obs|2))O(f_{1}^{2}/(f_{2}\cdot|\mathcal{P}_{\text{obs}}|^{2})) and is negligible for |𝒫obs|≥20|\mathcal{P}_{\text{obs}}|\geq 20 in practice.

State-space coverage (CstateC_{\text{state}}). Cstate=1−e−|π(𝒮obs)|/λC_{\text{state}}=1-e^{-|\pi(\mathcal{S}_{\text{obs}})|/\lambda}. Since |π⁡(𝒮obs)||\pi(\mathcal{S}_{\text{obs}})| can only increase (or stay the same) with additional test executions, and f(x)=1−e−x/λf(x)=1-e^{-x/\lambda} is monotonically increasing in xx, we have CstateC_{\text{state}} is non-decreasing.

Boundary coverage (CboundaryC_{\text{boundary}}). Cboundary=|ℬtested|/|ℬ|C_{\text{boundary}}=|\mathcal{B}_{\text{tested}}|/|\mathcal{B}|. Same argument as tool coverage: the numerator can only increase or stay the same, and the denominator is fixed.

Model coverage (CmodelC_{\text{model}}). Cmodel=|ℳtested|/|ℳtarget|C_{\text{model}}=|\mathcal{M}_{\text{tested}}|/|\mathcal{M}_{\text{target}}|. Same argument: numerator non-decreasing, denominator fixed.

Since each component CiC_{i} is non-decreasing, the tuple 𝒞⁡(𝒮)\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{S}) is component-wise non-decreasing. ∎

A.3 Proofs from Section 5

Proof of Theorem 5.1 (Mutation Adequacy).

We formalize the coupling effect assumption and use it to derive the detection probability bound.

Coupling Effect Assumption. For agent AA, a regression A→A∗A\to A^{*} with behavioral impact Δ⁡(A,A∗)=δ\Delta(A,A^{*})=\delta can be decomposed into a sequence of elementary perturbations, each corresponding to a mutation operator from ℳ\mathcal{M}. Formally, there exist mutations m1,…,mL∈ℳm_{1},\ldots,m_{L}\in\mathcal{M} such that:

A∗≈mL∘⋯∘m1(A)A^{*}\approx m_{L}\circ\cdots\circ m_{1}(A) (83)

where L=L⁡(δ)L=L(\delta) is the decomposition length and each mim_{i} has individual behavioral impact δi\delta_{i} with ∑δi≥δ\sum\delta_{i}\geq\delta.

Proof by contrapositive. Suppose the test suite 𝒮\mathcal{S} fails to detect the regression A→A∗A\to A^{*}. Then 𝒮\mathcal{S} does not detect any statistically significant difference between AA and A∗A^{*}.

By the coupling assumption, the regression decomposes into LL elementary mutations. The test suite has mutation score MS≥τ\text{MS}\geq\tau, so it kills a fraction τ\tau of all non-equivalent mutations.

For the test suite to miss the regression, it must fail to detect all constituent elementary mutations that contribute to the behavioral impact. The probability that a specific constituent mutation mim_{i} is not killed, conditioned on it being non-equivalent, is at most 1−τ1-\tau.

Under the independence approximation (kill decisions for different mutations are approximately independent), the probability that none of the LL constituent mutations are killed is:

ℙ⁡[all missed]≤(1−τ)L\mathbb{P}[\text{all missed}]\leq(1-\tau)^{L} (84)

The decomposition length LL relates to the impact δ\delta through the characteristic scale δ0\delta_{0} (the average impact of a single mutation):

L≥δδ0L\geq\frac{\delta}{\delta_{0}} (85)

Therefore:

ℙ[all missed]≤(1−τ)δ/δ0≤e−τ⋅δ/δ0\mathbb{P}[\text{all missed}]\leq(1-\tau)^{\delta/\delta_{0}}\leq e^{-\tau\cdot\delta/\delta_{0}} (86)

using the inequality 1−x≤e−x1-x\leq e^{-x} for x∈[0,1]x\in[0,1].

The detection probability is:

ℙ[𝒮 detects regression]=1−ℙ[all missed]≥1−e−τ⋅δ/δ0≥τ⋅(1−e−δ/δ0)\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{S}\text{ detects regression}]=1-\mathbb{P}[\text{all missed}]\geq 1-e^{-\tau\cdot\delta/\delta_{0}}\geq\tau\cdot(1-e^{-\delta/\delta_{0}}) (87)

The last inequality uses 1−e−x​y≥x⁡(1−e−y)1-e^{-xy}\geq x(1-e^{-y}) for x,y≥0x,y\geq 0, which follows from the concavity of 1−e−t1-e^{-t}. ∎

Proof of Corollary 5.2.

When MS=1\text{MS}=1 (all non-equivalent mutants killed), the detection probability from Theorem 5.1 becomes:

ℙ[detect]≥1⋅(1−e−δ/δ0)=1−e−δ/δ0\mathbb{P}[\text{detect}]\geq 1\cdot(1-e^{-\delta/\delta_{0}})=1-e^{-\delta/\delta_{0}} (88)

As δ/δ0→∞\delta/\delta_{0}\to\infty (the regression impact is much larger than the characteristic mutation scale):

ℙ[detect]≥1−e−δ/δ0→1\mathbb{P}[\text{detect}]\geq 1-e^{-\delta/\delta_{0}}\to 1 (89)

This confirms that a maximally adequate test suite (MS =1=1) under complete mutation operators will detect any sufficiently large regression with probability approaching 1. ∎

A.4 Proofs from Section 7

Proof of Proposition 7.4 (Multi-Fidelity Cost Reduction).

We adapt the multi-fidelity Monte Carlo framework of Peherstorfer et al. [28] to the hypothesis testing setting.

Setup. Let AeA_{e} and AcA_{c} be agents using models MeM_{e} and McM_{c} with per-trial costs cec_{e} and ccc_{c} respectively. Let 𝐟e=F⁡(τe)\mathbf{f}_{e}=F(\tau_{e}) and 𝐟c=F⁡(τc)\mathbf{f}_{c}=F(\tau_{c}) be their behavioral fingerprints, with correlation ρ=Corr⁡(𝐟e,𝐟c)\rho=\mathrm{Corr}(\mathbf{f}_{e},\mathbf{f}_{c}).

Control variate formulation. The multi-fidelity estimator for the mean fingerprint of AeA_{e} uses AcA_{c} as a control variate:

𝝁^mf=1ne​∑i=1ne𝐟e(i)+ρ^​(1nc​∑j=1nc𝐟c(j)−1ne​∑i=1ne𝐟c(i))\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\mathrm{mf}}=\frac{1}{n_{e}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{e}}\mathbf{f}_{e}^{(i)}+\hat{\rho}\left(\frac{1}{n_{c}}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{c}}\mathbf{f}_{c}^{(j)}-\frac{1}{n_{e}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{e}}\mathbf{f}_{c}^{(i)}\right) (90)

where ρ^\hat{\rho} is the estimated correlation and the second sum uses paired proxy evaluations on the same inputs as the target trials.

The variance of this estimator is:

Var⁡[𝝁^mf]=σe2ne​(1−ρ2)+ρ2​σc2nc\mathrm{Var}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\mathrm{mf}}]=\frac{\sigma_{e}^{2}}{n_{e}}(1-\rho^{2})+\frac{\rho^{2}\sigma_{c}^{2}}{n_{c}} (91)

Optimal allocation. The total cost is 𝒞=ne​ce+nc​cc\mathcal{C}=n_{e}c_{e}+n_{c}c_{c}. We minimize 𝒞\mathcal{C} subject to Var⁡[𝝁^mf]≤σtarget2\mathrm{Var}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\mathrm{mf}}]\leq\sigma^{2}_{\mathrm{target}} where σtarget2\sigma^{2}_{\mathrm{target}} is the variance required for power 1−β1-\beta.

Using Lagrange multipliers, the optimal ratio is:

nc∗ne∗=ρ​ce​σc2cc​σe2\frac{n_{c}^{*}}{n_{e}^{*}}=\rho\sqrt{\frac{c_{e}\sigma_{c}^{2}}{c_{c}\sigma_{e}^{2}}} (92)

Cost ratio. The total cost with optimal allocation, relative to single-fidelity testing with nsinglen_{\mathrm{single}} target trials, is:

ne∗​ce+nc∗​ccnsingle​ce\displaystyle\frac{n_{e}^{*}c_{e}+n_{c}^{*}c_{c}}{n_{\mathrm{single}}c_{e}} =(1−ρ2)+ρ2​cc/ce⋅σc2/σe21\displaystyle=\frac{(1-\rho^{2})+\rho^{2}\sqrt{c_{c}/c_{e}}\cdot\sqrt{\sigma_{c}^{2}/\sigma_{e}^{2}}}{1} (93)
≤1−ρ2+ρ2​cc/ce\displaystyle\leq 1-\rho^{2}+\rho^{2}\sqrt{c_{c}/c_{e}} (94)

where the inequality assumes σc≤σe\sigma_{c}\leq\sigma_{e} (the proxy model is at most as variable as the target).

For cc/ce≤0.01c_{c}/c_{e}\leq 0.01 (a 100×\times cost difference, common for mini vs. full models):

Cost ratio≤1−ρ2+0.1​ρ2=1−0.9​ρ2\text{Cost ratio}\leq 1-\rho^{2}+0.1\rho^{2}=1-0.9\rho^{2} (95)

Combined evidence. The pp-values pep_{e} and pcp_{c} from the target and proxy tests are combined via Fisher’s method with correlation weighting. Under H0H_{0}, −2​log⁡pe∼χ22-2\log p_{e}\sim\chi^{2}_{2} and −2​log⁡pc∼χ22-2\log p_{c}\sim\chi^{2}_{2}. The weighted combination:

χcombined2=−2​[ρ​log⁡pc+(1−ρ)​log⁡pe]\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{combined}}=-2[\rho\log p_{c}+(1-\rho)\log p_{e}] (96)

is approximately χ42\chi^{2}_{4} under H0H_{0} when pep_{e} and pcp_{c} are approximately independent conditional on the true parameter. The approximation improves as ne,ncn_{e},n_{c} grow. Under H1H_{1}, the non-centrality increases, providing greater power than either test alone.

Numerical verification. For ρ=0.8\rho=0.8, cc/ce=0.1c_{c}/c_{e}=0.1: cost ratio =1−0.9×0.64=0.424=1-0.9\times 0.64=0.424, giving 2.4×\times savings. For ρ=0.9\rho=0.9: cost ratio =1−0.9×0.81=0.271=1-0.9\times 0.81=0.271, giving 3.7×\times savings. ∎

Proof of Proposition 7.5 (Warm-Start Efficiency).

We prove each part of the proposition.

Part (1): Error control.

The warm-start SPRT initializes at Λ0warm\Lambda_{0}^{\mathrm{warm}} instead of 00. The key observation is that the Bayesian prior update is consistent with the likelihood ratio: if the prior accurately reflects the distribution of pp, then:

Λ0warm=log⁡B⁡(θ−δ,a0,b0)B⁡(θ,a0,b0)=log⁡ℙ⁡[p=θ−δ∣prior data]ℙ⁡[p=θ∣prior data]\Lambda_{0}^{\mathrm{warm}}=\log\frac{B(\theta-\delta;a_{0},b_{0})}{B(\theta;a_{0},b_{0})}=\log\frac{\mathbb{P}[p=\theta-\delta\mid\text{prior data}]}{\mathbb{P}[p=\theta\mid\text{prior data}]} (97)

This is the Bayes factor from the prior data. When the prior is well-calibrated (generated from the same agent version or a version with |pv−pv′|≤δ/2|p_{v}-p_{v^{\prime}}|\leq\delta/2), the initial position Λ0warm\Lambda_{0}^{\mathrm{warm}} is between the boundaries aa and bb with high probability, and the subsequent SPRT updates maintain the standard error control by Wald’s identity:

ℙ⁡[cross ​a∣H0]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[\text{cross }a\mid H_{0}] =ℙ⁡[ΛNwarm≤a∣H0]\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}[\Lambda_{N}^{\mathrm{warm}}\leq a\mid H_{0}] (98)
≤ea1=β1−α≤α\displaystyle\leq\frac{e^{a}}{1}=\frac{\beta}{1-\alpha}\leq\alpha (99)

The same argument holds for Type II error with boundary bb.

Part (2): Sample savings.

The warm-start SPRT is equivalent to a standard SPRT that has already accumulated evidence Λ0warm\Lambda_{0}^{\mathrm{warm}}. By Wald’s equation:

𝔼⁡[ΛNwarm∣Hi]=Λ0warm+𝔼⁡[Nwarm]⋅𝔼⁡[λ1∣Hi]\mathbb{E}[\Lambda_{N}^{\mathrm{warm}}\mid H_{i}]=\Lambda_{0}^{\mathrm{warm}}+\mathbb{E}[N_{\mathrm{warm}}]\cdot\mathbb{E}[\lambda_{1}\mid H_{i}] (100)

Since 𝔼⁡[ΛNwarm]\mathbb{E}[\Lambda_{N}^{\mathrm{warm}}] equals the same boundary expectations as the cold-start SPRT, we have:

Λ0warm+𝔼⁡[Nwarm]⋅𝔼⁡[λ1∣Hi]\displaystyle\Lambda_{0}^{\mathrm{warm}}+\mathbb{E}[N_{\mathrm{warm}}]\cdot\mathbb{E}[\lambda_{1}\mid H_{i}] =𝔼⁡[Ncold]⋅𝔼⁡[λ1∣Hi]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[N_{\mathrm{cold}}]\cdot\mathbb{E}[\lambda_{1}\mid H_{i}] (101)
𝔼⁡[Nwarm]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[N_{\mathrm{warm}}] =𝔼⁡[Ncold]−Λ0warm𝔼⁡[λ1∣Hi]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[N_{\mathrm{cold}}]-\frac{\Lambda_{0}^{\mathrm{warm}}}{\mathbb{E}[\lambda_{1}\mid H_{i}]} (102)

When testing under H0H_{0} (p=θp=\theta), 𝔼⁡[λ1∣H0]<0\mathbb{E}[\lambda_{1}\mid H_{0}]<0 (the LLR drifts toward boundary bb). If the prior correctly supports H0H_{0}, then Λ0warm>0\Lambda_{0}^{\mathrm{warm}}>0, giving:

𝔼⁡[Nwarm]=𝔼⁡[Ncold]−|Λ0warm||𝔼⁡[λ1∣H0]|≤𝔼⁡[Ncold]\mathbb{E}[N_{\mathrm{warm}}]=\mathbb{E}[N_{\mathrm{cold}}]-\frac{|\Lambda_{0}^{\mathrm{warm}}|}{|\mathbb{E}[\lambda_{1}\mid H_{0}]|}\leq\mathbb{E}[N_{\mathrm{cold}}] (103)

The savings |Λ0warm|/|𝔼⁡[λ1]||\Lambda_{0}^{\mathrm{warm}}|/|\mathbb{E}[\lambda_{1}]| represent the number of trials’ worth of evidence contained in the prior.

Part (3): Graceful degradation.

If the prior is mis-calibrated, Λ0warm\Lambda_{0}^{\mathrm{warm}} may be on the wrong side of zero. In the worst case, it pushes the random walk closer to the wrong boundary. The excess error probability is bounded by the likelihood ratio at the initial position.

For a Type I error under mis-calibration:

ℙ[cross a∣H0,mis-calibrated]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[\text{cross }a\mid H_{0},\text{mis-calibrated}] ≤ℙ⁡[cross ​a∣H0]⋅e|Λ0warm|\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}[\text{cross }a\mid H_{0}]\cdot e^{|\Lambda_{0}^{\mathrm{warm}}|} (104)

by the submartingale maximal inequality applied to the likelihood ratio process. Since ℙ⁡[cross ​a∣H0]≤α\mathbb{P}[\text{cross }a\mid H_{0}]\leq\alpha for the well-calibrated case:

α′≤α⋅e|Λ0warm|\alpha^{\prime}\leq\alpha\cdot e^{|\Lambda_{0}^{\mathrm{warm}}|} (105)

For moderate priors (n0≤20n_{0}\leq 20), the initial position is bounded by |Λ0warm|≤n0⋅maxr⁡|λ⁡(r)|≈n0⋅|log⁡(θ/(θ−δ))|≈2|\Lambda_{0}^{\mathrm{warm}}|\leq n_{0}\cdot\max_{r}|\lambda(r)|\approx n_{0}\cdot|\log(\theta/(\theta-\delta))|\approx 2 for typical θ=0.9\theta=0.9, δ=0.1\delta=0.1. This gives e|Λ0warm|≤e2≈7.4e^{|\Lambda_{0}^{\mathrm{warm}}|}\leq e^{2}\approx 7.4, so α′≤7.4​α=0.37\alpha^{\prime}\leq 7.4\alpha=0.37 in the extreme worst case. In practice, the mis-calibration factor is much smaller because priors are typically close to correct. For n0=10n_{0}=10 with a version that differs by ≤δ/2\leq\delta/2, the mis-calibration factor is typically ≤1.5\leq 1.5, giving α′≤1.5​α\alpha^{\prime}\leq 1.5\alpha. ∎
